scenarios.title: Leave room beside the screen
scenarios.objective: Support a net-front teammate without occupying the same shooting lane.
scenarios.briefing: Navy attacks +x. F1 is near the right net-front lane, YOU is to the side, D1 marks the middle, and the goalie is set. The rep asks for a useful support relationship, not a fixed net-front spot.
cues: F1 is the puck carrier near the net-front lane.
YOU has space beside the carrier and goalie.

questions.prompt: Which navy player is closest to the net-front lane?

options.text: YOU
F1
D1

questions.explanation: F1 is the navy puck carrier closest to the goalie; YOU is beside the play.

questions.prompt: Which two questions clarify YOU's support job?

options.text: Can F1 see a reachable pass to YOU?
Would YOU leave the direct shooting lane open?
Should YOU stand on top of F1?

questions.explanation: Support is useful when F1 can reach it and the lane stays distinct; crowding F1 removes both choices.

questions.prompt: Arrange this net-front support read.

options.text: Locate F1, D1 and the goalie
Choose space beside the shooting lane
Re-check the pass and shot lanes

questions.explanation: The support spot depends on the carrier, defender, and goalie relationships, then changes with the next play.

questions.prompt: Move YOU beside the shooting lane, away from F1 and D1.
questions.explanation: This point leaves F1 in the lane and gives YOU a separate support angle.

questions.prompt: F1 turns to pass instead of shooting. What should YOU check?

options.text: Whether the pass reaches you without pulling D1 into the lane
Stay still because the shot lane is unchanged
Move across F1's stick lane

questions.explanation: The carrier changed from shot to pass, so check reachability and D1's reaction before offering the same spot.

questions.prompt: How would you describe “beside the shot lane” to a teammate?
questions.explanation: Name F1, the goalie, and D1, then describe space that gives F1 a route while leaving the direct lane readable. Adjust if the defender follows.

scenarios.title: Protect the inside gap
scenarios.objective: Defend the middle while matching the carrier's changing speed and support.
scenarios.briefing: Gold attacks -x. Navy YOU defends the right net; F1 carries toward the net with F2 wide. YOU starts inside F1's route, with the goalie behind.
cues: Gold F1 carries toward the right net.
YOU starts inside the carrier route.
F2 is wide support; the middle remains the priority cue.

questions.prompt: Which net is YOU defending in this gold attack?

options.text: The left net
The right net
Both nets at once

questions.explanation: Gold attacks -x toward the left, so Navy defends the right net at +x in this diagram.

questions.prompt: What should your gap relate to?

options.text: F1's speed and route
The space between F1 and the right net
A fixed distance that ignores movement

questions.explanation: Gap control connects carrier speed, route, and net protection; one number does not describe the changing picture.

questions.prompt: Arrange this inside-gap read.

options.text: Protect the middle and net
Match F1's route and speed
Re-check F2 and the next lane

questions.explanation: Start with the dangerous middle, then match the carrier and update support.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to an inside position between F1 and the right net.
questions.explanation: This point stays between the carrier and the net while preserving a view of F2.

questions.prompt: F1 gains the outside of YOU. What must update?

options.text: The recovery route and the space between F1 and the net
Keep the original gap as if F1 stayed inside
Chase F2 and leave F1 alone

questions.explanation: F1's route changed the immediate threat. Recover toward the net while re-reading F2 and your support.

questions.prompt: Why is there no single correct gap number here?
questions.explanation: F1's speed, route, and distance to the net change the useful relationship. Explain the visible cue that would make you close or contain.

scenarios.title: Guide the carrier to the wall
scenarios.objective: Use an inside angle to influence the carrier away from the middle without guessing the outcome.
scenarios.briefing: Gold attacks -x. F1 carries along the right side toward Navy's net; YOU is inside the route, F2 trails wide, and the goalie is behind. The angle must follow the carrier's changes.
cues: F1 is wide on the right.
F2 trails on the far side.

questions.prompt: Where is YOU compared with wide F1?

options.text: Outside F1 toward the wall
Inside F1 toward the middle
Behind the goalie

questions.explanation: YOU is inside the wider F1 relative to the goal-side route; the named relationship matters more than a dot.

questions.prompt: What does an inside approach try to preserve?

options.text: The middle and the route to the net
A chance to chase F2 wide immediately
A predictable carrier path regardless of movement

questions.explanation: Inside positioning protects the middle and route to the net while showing the carrier a wall-side route; F2 remains a separate scan, not an immediate chase.

questions.prompt: Arrange this angling read.

options.text: Find F1's route and the middle
Match the inside relationship
Update if F1 cuts back

questions.explanation: Angling is a relationship that must be updated when the carrier changes direction.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to an inside approach that remains between F1 and the middle.
questions.explanation: This point keeps YOU inside the wide carrier while leaving room to update the angle.

questions.prompt: F1 cuts back toward centre ice. What should you reassess?

options.text: Your inside relationship and the space F1 now wants
Continue toward the wall as if F1 stayed wide
Follow F2 instead of the carrier

questions.explanation: The cut-back changes F1's route and the inside gap. Re-match the carrier while protecting the middle.

questions.prompt: How would you describe this angle using the slot and half wall?
questions.explanation: Say that YOU stays between F1 and the slot, showing the half-wall route while watching the carrier's cut-back and F2.

scenarios.title: Recover toward the net
scenarios.objective: Recover to a useful net-side relationship after a first reach does not win the puck.
scenarios.briefing: Gold attacks -x. F1 has moved ahead of YOU toward the left net; F2 is farther wide. YOU is behind the play and the goalie is visible. The first reach is stated to have missed.
cues: F1 is ahead toward the left net.
F2 is a separate wide threat.

questions.prompt: Which attacker has moved beyond YOU toward the left net?

options.text: F1
F2
The goalie

questions.explanation: The briefing identifies F1 as ahead of YOU toward the left net.

questions.prompt: Which two details guide a useful recovery?

options.text: F1's route to the net
F2's separate wide position
A second reach from behind even if the picture changes

questions.explanation: The carrier route and second attacker shape recovery. A repeated reach may leave the net-side relationship worse.

questions.prompt: Arrange the recovery response.

options.text: Recognize the missed reach
Recover toward the net-side space
Re-check F1 and F2

questions.explanation: The response prioritizes a useful relationship and then updates both attackers.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to a recovery point between the attackers and the left net.
questions.explanation: This point moves toward the defended net-side lane and keeps F2 visible across the ice.

questions.prompt: F1 slows toward the boards while F2 drives middle. What should update?

options.text: Your recovery should protect the new middle threat while staying connected to F1
Keep chasing F1 into the boards
Ignore F2 because the first reach was on F1

questions.explanation: F1 and F2 changed jobs in the picture. Protect the middle and keep a playable relationship to F1.

questions.prompt: Why can recovering toward the net be better than reaching again from behind?
questions.explanation: The net-side relationship limits the dangerous lane and keeps both attackers in view. A second reach may miss and leave the middle unprotected.

scenarios.title: Backcheck the open runner
scenarios.objective: Choose a backcheck relationship for the uncovered attacker while a teammate pressures the puck.
scenarios.briefing: Gold attacks -x. F1 carries toward the left net and D1 is already pressuring F1. F2 trails on the far side; YOU is behind both attackers and must scan F2 rather than simply chase the puck.
cues: F2 is the uncovered trailing attacker.

options.text: F2’s route toward the left net
D1's ability to stay with F1
The puck alone, without scanning F2

questions.explanation: The uncovered runner toward the left net and D1’s pressure on F1 define the backcheck job.

questions.prompt: Arrange this backcheck check-in.

options.text: Find F2 and the right net
Skate into a useful relationship
Re-check F1, F2 and D1

questions.explanation: The route protects the open runner, then updates as the teammate pressure changes.

questions.prompt: Move YOU toward F2 while staying between F2 and the left net.
questions.explanation: This point closes the defended net-side relationship to F2 without pretending that one spot solves the play.

questions.prompt: D1 falls behind F1 and calls for help. How should YOU respond?

options.text: Keep F2 in view while deciding whether the carrier now needs support
Leave both attackers to chase the puck
Stay on F2 without checking F1

questions.explanation: D1's changed position may shift the job. Re-scan both attackers and support the more dangerous reachable lane.

questions.prompt: How is a backcheck different from simply skating toward the puck?
questions.explanation: It connects your route to an attacker and the net, so you can limit a pass or shot while reading the teammate pressure.
